strengths: Addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: repeated stimuli and overlapping signal windows can undermine claims of generalization in brain-to-text decoding. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b04/review-experiment-jtrosg_5/call-0848a65663964df5bf81ec3899b5e70a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The taxonomy of splitting methods and subject–stimulus graph formulation help clarify evaluation assumptions. Grouping fMRI samples by story sensibly addresses overlapping temporal windows.

Experiments cover two modalities, two public datasets, and two relevant model architectures. Four splitting seeds support the overlap analysis, and the large reported performance differences motivate closer examination of existing protocols.
weaknesses: The published algorithms do not enforce the central separation guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, adds edges for training subjects without excluding validation/test stimuli; Algorithm 2, line 33, analogously fails to exclude held-out subjects. These expansion steps can reintroduce contamination. The pseudocode also conflicts with the prose about which vertices receive one initial edge. A corrected implementation and explicit checks of pairwise disjointness are necessary.

The experiments do not establish that decoder memorization explains the performance differences. Table 2 changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration simultaneously, while different splits change evaluation difficulty and potentially training-set size. Random initialization is not a no-signal control. Matched training conditions and text-only or shuffled-signal controls are needed, alongside clarification of whether evaluation uses free-running generation or reference prefixes.

The interpretation of learning curves is unsound. Decreasing validation reconstruction loss does not establish encoder overfitting or degradation, and improving generation scores with additional training does not independently diagnose contamination. The leakage-free EEG setting also exhibits declining validation loss. These observations require direct generalization tests rather than the causal conclusions drawn in Section 4.4.

Metric definitions and numerical reporting need correction. Equations 7–8 use sample intersections to describe subject/text reuse and normalize by training counts, leaving their stated interpretation as test leakage fractions unclear. Table 3 reports ROUGE-1 F=84.64 with precision=63.16 and recall=71.50, which is impossible under standard consistent aggregation; even the arithmetic-mean upper bound is 67.33.

Holding out both subjects and stimuli appropriately evaluates the stated joint generalization target, but the condemnation of all subject overlap as contamination is too broad. Shared participants can be legitimate in subject-specific decoding. The paper should distinguish evaluation of a different deployment setting from actual sample leakage and restrict its conclusions accordingly.

The benchmark is insufficiently specified for reproduction. Although some hyperparameters are provided, the manuscript supplies no benchmark artifact link, exact split assignments, retained/discarded sample counts, realized split proportions, or uncertainty estimates for generation results. Four seeds for overlap statistics do not establish robustness of model comparisons. Together with the algorithmic and experimental issues, these gaps require correction and controlled reruns before a Findings recommendation is justified.
